# Scott Christensen: Growth Design Leader

- Source URL: https://scottchristensen.design/
- Markdown URL: https://scottchristensen.design/index.md
- Site index for agents: https://scottchristensen.design/llms.txt
- Retrieved: 2026-11-09

> Portfolio home for Scott Christensen, growth design leader and SendSight cofounder: current focus, selected case studies, background, and experience.

## About Scott

Scott Christensen is a growth design leader based in Salt Lake City with 15 years of experience connecting design craft to strategy and growth. He is cofounder of [SendSight](https://sendsight.ai), which automates lifecycle journey insights for growth teams.

Previously: Design Lead, Growth at [Mercury](https://mercury.com) (2023–2025); Head of Product Design at [H1](https://h1.co) (2020–2022); Founding Designer at [Mystery](https://www.trymystery.com) (2019–2020); Lead Designer / Design Manager at Egencia, an Expedia company (2018–2019); Product Designer / Sr. Designer at PwC Experience Center (2015–2018); Management Consultant at PwC's Strategy& (2013–2015). He helped start [GrowthDesigners.co](https://growthdesigners.co), a community for growth designers, by creating its Slack community in 2018, and has spent about eight years helping build it to 2,000+ members. He also co-leads [Growth Design School](https://www.growthdesigners.co/school), the community's growth design course.

Education: Brigham Young University (BYU), business strategy, graduated 2013. He moved from management consulting into design and is self-taught as a designer.

Profiles: [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/scottcharleschristensen/) · [X @_ScottC_](https://x.com/_ScottC_) · [GitHub](https://github.com/scottchristensen) · [Medium @ScottC](https://medium.com/@ScottC)

Not to be confused with other people named Scott Christensen, including a painter of the same name. This Scott Christensen is the product and growth designer described on scottchristensen.design.

## Now

Building [SendSight](https://sendsight.ai) to surface lifecycle journey insights for growth teams.

## Selected work

- [SendSight](https://scottchristensen.design/work/sendsight/): Making lifecycle programs visible
- [Mercury Focused Funding](https://scottchristensen.design/work/mercury-focused-funding/): Adding friction lifted Day 30 deposits 7%
- [Mercury Viral Upsell](https://scottchristensen.design/work/mercury-viral-upsell/): Layered education lifted new accounts 6%
- [Mystery Onboarding](https://scottchristensen.design/work/mystery-onboarding/): Data-driven new user flow

## About

At Mercury, the banking platform for startups, Scott led growth design focused on activation, and helped launch new products including Mercury's Slack app and financial SaaS for Bill Pay and Invoicing.

At H1 he was head of product design, joining at Series A and scaling the design team to six as a player-coach. Before that he was founding designer at Mystery, an entertainment marketplace.

He began his career at PwC building zero-to-one products, then led growth initiatives and managed a team at Expedia.

Outside work: dad life with his toddlers, endurance sports, and the mountains near his home in Salt Lake City.

# Content: talks, podcasts, writing, and community

> Scott's interviews and talks on growth design careers and product-led growth, the GrowthDesigners.co community and Growth Design School he built, his newsletter and Medium writing, and free Figma resources.

## About Scott

Scott Christensen is a growth design leader based in Salt Lake City with 15 years of experience connecting design craft to strategy and growth. He is cofounder of [SendSight](https://sendsight.ai), which automates lifecycle journey insights for growth teams.

Previously: Design Lead, Growth at [Mercury](https://mercury.com) (2023–2025); Head of Product Design at [H1](https://h1.co) (2020–2022); Founding Designer at [Mystery](https://www.trymystery.com) (2019–2020); Lead Designer / Design Manager at Egencia, an Expedia company (2018–2019); Product Designer / Sr. Designer at PwC Experience Center (2015–2018); Management Consultant at PwC's Strategy& (2013–2015). He helped start [GrowthDesigners.co](https://growthdesigners.co), a community for growth designers, by creating its Slack community in 2018, and has spent about eight years helping build it to 2,000+ members. He also co-leads [Growth Design School](https://www.growthdesigners.co/school), the community's growth design course.

Education: Brigham Young University (BYU), business strategy, graduated 2013. He moved from management consulting into design and is self-taught as a designer.

Profiles: [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/scottcharleschristensen/) · [X @_ScottC_](https://x.com/_ScottC_) · [GitHub](https://github.com/scottchristensen) · [Medium @ScottC](https://medium.com/@ScottC)

Not to be confused with other people named Scott Christensen, including a painter of the same name. This Scott Christensen is the product and growth designer described on scottchristensen.design.

## Interviews and talks

### [Beyond UX Design: Broad Strokes Before Fine Lines](https://www.beyonduxdesign.com/episode/92-the-generalists-advantage-with-scott-christensen/)
August 2024 · podcast with Jeremy Miller · 58 min. Published as ep. 92, "The Generalist's Advantage". Recorded while Scott was lead growth designer at Mercury. He argues against niching down early in a UX career and proposes a career "double diamond": go broad first, then specialise. Topics include a competence framework, "there are no gatekeepers: gatekeep yourself", the skills a well-rounded UX designer needs, how to choose what to specialise in, and three heuristics for knowing whether you're a good growth designer.

### [Design Growth Podcast: Episode 19 with Scott Christensen (by TryMata)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6bLtMl8dZhM)
July 2023 · livestream.

### [SaaStock Presentation with Jonathan Anderson, CEO @ Candu.ai](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RiGEkgsUFdk)
June 2023 · Austin, TX · 14 min. Published as "PLG Activation Best Practices". Scott and Jonathan Anderson tear down Airtable's onboarding flow to illustrate product-led-growth activation practices.

### [Growth Design at Startups, with Emmanuel Omole](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/04-growth-designer-at-early-stage-startup-scott-christensen/id1659270905?i=1000605939008)
March 2023 · podcast with Emmanuel Omole · 37 min. Published as Grow the Product, ep. 4, "Growth Designer at Early-Stage Startup". Recorded while Scott ran his own growth design consultancy. Covers the stages of a startup and what each means for growth, what a growth designer should look for when deciding which startup to join, how to hone your craft at an early-stage company, and go-to-market considerations.

### [Is Early-Stage Growth Design for You? with Ran Liu](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Lz6W4Fq3Msk)
March 2023 · live broadcast · 59 min. GrowthDesigners.co community event, published as "Is Early-Stage Startup Meant for You?". A live discussion following Scott's March 2023 GrowthDesigners newsletter: how growth differs at early vs. later-stage companies, whether you'll hone your craft as a growth designer at an early-stage company, and what to look for when choosing a startup.

## Community: GrowthDesigners.co

[GrowthDesigners.co](https://growthdesigners.co) is a community for designers focused on blending growth strategy and design to make a lasting business impact. Scott helped start it by creating the Slack community in 2018, and has helped build it to 2,000+ members over about eight years. It offers a Slack community for asynchronous discussion, mentorship, and free events, a monthly newsletter on growth design topics, and Growth Design School.

[Growth Design School](https://www.growthdesigners.co/school) launched in 2023. It's a remote growth design masterclass: about 5 hours of video, case studies, assignments, and live debriefs, covering foundations, the scientific design process, acquisition, activation and engagement, conversion, and ethical design. Scott co-leads and teaches it with Chase Denomme and Molly Norris Walker.

# SendSight: case study

- Source URL: https://scottchristensen.design/work/sendsight/
- Markdown URL: https://scottchristensen.design/work/sendsight.md
- Site index for agents: https://scottchristensen.design/llms.txt
- Retrieved: 2026-11-09

> Making lifecycle programs visible. I co-founded SendSight to give growth teams visibility into the lifecycle messages they send.

## About Scott

Scott Christensen is a growth design leader based in Salt Lake City with 15 years of experience connecting design craft to strategy and growth. He is cofounder of [SendSight](https://sendsight.ai), which automates lifecycle journey insights for growth teams.

Previously: Design Lead, Growth at [Mercury](https://mercury.com) (2023–2025); Head of Product Design at [H1](https://h1.co) (2020–2022); Founding Designer at [Mystery](https://www.trymystery.com) (2019–2020); Lead Designer / Design Manager at Egencia, an Expedia company (2018–2019); Product Designer / Sr. Designer at PwC Experience Center (2015–2018); Management Consultant at PwC's Strategy& (2013–2015). He helped start [GrowthDesigners.co](https://growthdesigners.co), a community for growth designers, by creating its Slack community in 2018, and has spent about eight years helping build it to 2,000+ members. He also co-leads [Growth Design School](https://www.growthdesigners.co/school), the community's growth design course.

Education: Brigham Young University (BYU), business strategy, graduated 2013. He moved from management consulting into design and is self-taught as a designer.

Profiles: [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/scottcharleschristensen/) · [X @_ScottC_](https://x.com/_ScottC_) · [GitHub](https://github.com/scottchristensen) · [Medium @ScottC](https://medium.com/@ScottC)

Not to be confused with other people named Scott Christensen, including a painter of the same name. This Scott Christensen is the product and growth designer described on scottchristensen.design.

## At a glance

- **Project:** SendSight: Making lifecycle programs visible
- **Scott's role:** Co-founder, Design, front end, positioning & sales
- **Team:** 1 x Co-founder (engineering)
- **Year / duration:** 2025 – present
- **Category:** zero-to-one; growth

## Overview

I co-founded [SendSight](https://sendsight.ai) to give growth teams visibility into the lifecycle messages they send. Proper case study work in progress, but here's the backstory.

## Background

*(Interactive demo: [SendSight interactive demo](https://app.sendsight.ai/demo))*

### Where it started

I came up with SendSight while leading growth design at [Mercury](https://mercury.com). I was mapping our in-product and lifecycle emails so they'd feel like one experience, and I hit the same wall I'd hit at Expedia and everywhere else: nobody had a clear picture of which emails were going out, to whom, and why. The answer lived in an ESP only a few marketers could log into.

I believe lifecycle email is part of the product. It's often the first and last thing a user sees from you, yet product teams rarely know what's being sent. The usual workaround is to screenshot every email into Figma and stitch the journeys together by hand, which leaves you with a map that's out of date the day it's finished.

### Taking the leap

I kept hearing the same pain in growth and lifecycle Slack communities, but nobody was solving it. One company had tried: Plot was venture-funded in 2020 and shut down in 2024. That told me the problem was real. It also made me doubt this was a venture-scale business, so we chose to bootstrap.

The final push came in November 2025. Working with Opus 4.5, I saw how quickly a small team could now build production software. I called Seth, a longtime friend who had been building production apps for clients at his AI consultancy. We were friends long before we were business partners, and our skills complement each other. I left to build SendSight full time.

### Figuring out who it's for

Before we wrote any production code, I designed a prototype of the vision and took it to customers. We talked with 100+ lifecycle marketers, growth leaders, and agencies in about three months. The pain ran deep enough that people would pay: our first paying pilots signed on before the real product existed, and we built the production version alongside them.

We came to lifecycle marketing as outsiders, and it took nine or ten months of calls and conferences before we felt we had our heads above water. We had planned a self-serve motion for small teams, but the pain hits hardest on large teams, where many people need visibility. That meant founder-led sales and enterprise procurement.

SendSight was also almost too abstract to explain. People couldn't picture what we were selling, and illustrated animations didn't help. So we put the real UI on the website with some parts locked down, which is how the demo above came about. It finally made clear what SendSight does.

### Designing the MCP

We built SendSight for lifecycle marketers. Then it started spreading inside customer organizations, because product managers and designers wanted to see what their users were receiving. So we leaned in, and I designed an MCP that lets anyone ask Claude about live journeys in plain language, without an ESP seat. There are no screens to design in an MCP. The design material is tool names, descriptions, and response shapes. The breakthrough was getting live journeys to render inline in the chat.

Wider access worried lifecycle teams, who didn't want their data misread, so I designed guardrails into it: a Viewer role, metrics labeled as lifetime snapshots, every claim linked back to its source, and drafts that stay private and never touch the ESP.

It's still early, and enterprise sales cycles run four to six months or more. At least a dozen times this year I thought we'd hit a dead end. Each time, we took the next step and found just enough validation to keep going.

# Mercury Focused Funding: case study

- Source URL: https://scottchristensen.design/work/mercury-focused-funding/
- Markdown URL: https://scottchristensen.design/work/mercury-focused-funding.md
- Site index for agents: https://scottchristensen.design/llms.txt
- Retrieved: 2026-11-09

> Adding friction lifted Day 30 deposits 7%. Mercury's deposit rate was plateauing despite a tidal wave of new applications after the Silicon Valley Bank collapse.

## About Scott

Scott Christensen is a growth design leader based in Salt Lake City with 15 years of experience connecting design craft to strategy and growth. He is cofounder of [SendSight](https://sendsight.ai), which automates lifecycle journey insights for growth teams.

Previously: Design Lead, Growth at [Mercury](https://mercury.com) (2023–2025); Head of Product Design at [H1](https://h1.co) (2020–2022); Founding Designer at [Mystery](https://www.trymystery.com) (2019–2020); Lead Designer / Design Manager at Egencia, an Expedia company (2018–2019); Product Designer / Sr. Designer at PwC Experience Center (2015–2018); Management Consultant at PwC's Strategy& (2013–2015). He helped start [GrowthDesigners.co](https://growthdesigners.co), a community for growth designers, by creating its Slack community in 2018, and has spent about eight years helping build it to 2,000+ members. He also co-leads [Growth Design School](https://www.growthdesigners.co/school), the community's growth design course.

Education: Brigham Young University (BYU), business strategy, graduated 2013. He moved from management consulting into design and is self-taught as a designer.

Profiles: [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/scottcharleschristensen/) · [X @_ScottC_](https://x.com/_ScottC_) · [GitHub](https://github.com/scottchristensen) · [Medium @ScottC](https://medium.com/@ScottC)

Not to be confused with other people named Scott Christensen, including a painter of the same name. This Scott Christensen is the product and growth designer described on scottchristensen.design.

## At a glance

- **Project:** Mercury Focused Funding: Adding friction lifted Day 30 deposits 7%
- **Scott's role:** Lead Growth Designer, Activation
- **Team:** 1 x Growth PM (interim), 1 x Growth Engineer, 1 x Junior Designer, 1 x Data Scientist, 7 x Engineers
- **Year / duration:** 2024 / 2 tests over 6 months
- **Category:** growth

## Overview

[Mercury](https://mercury.com)'s deposit rate was plateauing despite a tidal wave of new applications after the [Silicon Valley Bank collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_Silicon_Valley_Bank). I redesigned the focused-funding flow with deliberate friction, and lifted Day 30 deposits by 7% (relative lift). That added **~$2.3M ARR** 🎉.

## Background

[Mercury](https://mercury.com) is a fintech serving startups and SMBs that offers financial-management software on top of a core banking product. In early 2023, the Silicon Valley Bank collapse sent a tidal wave of new applications our way. But the conversion math wasn't keeping up: only **~59% of approved applicants actually deposited**. Leadership made a strategic growth bet to capture the high-intent users coming through the door before that wave subsided.

The pre-existing UX was passive and let users wander in with a dashboard module, empty states, and upsells across the product. The bet I was making: that wasn't forceful enough.

### The problem

- ~41% of approved applicants never funded their account
- Mercury is functionally useless without a deposit. Every other feature is downstream of having money in the account
- Activation was the highest-intent moment we'd ever have with these users, and we were leaving it to chance

### Team goals

The growth team had three concurrent goals: grow deposit *rate*, deposit *quality* (amount), and grow invoicing adoption. The focused-funding work touched all three.

## Process

### Discovery

I started by interviewing both funded and unfunded approved applicants. The hypothesis I was most worried about: that a forceful funding gate would feel constraining and people would bail.

The interviews flipped that. Funded users *didn't even remember* the funding moment of their flow. It was just part of opening a bank account. Unfunded users said something similar in concept: of course you'd have to deposit at some point. You're a bank.

> Mercury isn't valuable if you don't deposit money into it. Despite all the cool features we offer, none of them matter without funds in the account.

This is the kind of friction growth designers usually avoid. The team agreed it was the one moment in the funnel where a full-stop is justified.

### V1: The bet

We couldn't get full political buy-in for a hard gate up front, so we hedged: a small cohort test (20% of users) to read the directional impact. Even at that sample size, v1 lifted deposit rates significantly, enough to greenlight a broader rollout.

### Modal: full takeover vs. embedded

We explored a full-screen modal takeover but landed on an *embedded* modal that teases the dashboard underneath. Even with friction, you want users to remember what they're working toward.

*(Figma: Modal explorations: takeover vs. embedded)*

### Funding method hierarchy

The earliest iterations showed every funding method at equal weight on a single screen. After testing, I broke the flow into more steps with bigger click targets and one decision per screen. *More steps isn't always worse*. Conversational flows with one question at a time beat the dense single-screen layout in usability tests.

*(Figma: Multivariant test: control vs. 2 funding methods vs. 2 methods + invoicing)*

### V2: The refinements

Six months later, three things changed for the next round:

- **International wires.** A rising share of applicants were international, and they couldn't deposit in v1.
- **Mobile optimization.** Mobile traffic was growing too. v1 was desktop-first.
- **Invoicing as a funding method.** Multivariant test introducing invoicing to capture the professional-services cohort opening accounts to receive their first client payment, and to push on the company-wide invoicing-adoption goal. Result: **invoicing as a funding method went up 4%**.

*(Figma: Final shipped prototype (clickable))*

### Side win: the threshold-amount A/B

One idea I wanted in v1 but had to cut for speed: showing suggested deposit thresholds tied to what each amount *unlocks*. We came back to it as a fast-follow A/B test. Result: **+$1,500 to median deposit amount** on ACH and wire flows. Defaults are powerful; defaults *with a reason* are more powerful.

*(Figma: Funding-amount threshold multivariant)*

### Hard decision: going to bat for international wires

International wires almost got cut from v2: lower usage than ACH/domestic, hidden behind a progressive disclosure, lots of engineering complexity, and our interim PM had left before v2, so nobody was on hand to do the discovery. I took on the PM responsibilities myself, liaising with the wires & banking team, learning the nuances of cross-border transfers, doing the due diligence. International ended up being the single biggest driver of the v2 7% lift.

## Learnings

### Fill the gap

If something's blocking the work and the role isn't staffed, do the role. Taking on PM responsibilities for international wires felt risky at the time. It was the highest-leverage thing I did in this project.

### Pre-fill, and give users a reason why

The threshold-amount test wasn't just "here are some numbers." Each suggested amount mapped to a feature it unlocked. Defaults shape behavior. Defaults with rationale shape it more.

### More steps isn't always a bad thing

When each step is a clear, conversational question with big click targets, breaking a flow into more steps can *raise* completion rates. Density isn't speed. Clarity is speed.

### De-risk sensitive tests to win the room

Big growth bets are political. When the test you want to run is the kind detractors will push back on (a hard funding gate, in this case), a small-cohort pilot converts skeptics into believers faster than another deck does. The V1 cohort gave us a clean directional read without putting the funnel on the line. Once the numbers came in, the broader rollout sold itself.

# Mercury Viral Upsell: case study

- Source URL: https://scottchristensen.design/work/mercury-viral-upsell/
- Markdown URL: https://scottchristensen.design/work/mercury-viral-upsell.md
- Site index for agents: https://scottchristensen.design/llms.txt
- Retrieved: 2026-11-09

> Layered education lifted new accounts 6%. Mercury's viral upsell, the page non-Mercury users land on when a Mercury customer sends or requests money, was a slapped-together boilerplate form.

## About Scott

Scott Christensen is a growth design leader based in Salt Lake City with 15 years of experience connecting design craft to strategy and growth. He is cofounder of [SendSight](https://sendsight.ai), which automates lifecycle journey insights for growth teams.

Previously: Design Lead, Growth at [Mercury](https://mercury.com) (2023–2025); Head of Product Design at [H1](https://h1.co) (2020–2022); Founding Designer at [Mystery](https://www.trymystery.com) (2019–2020); Lead Designer / Design Manager at Egencia, an Expedia company (2018–2019); Product Designer / Sr. Designer at PwC Experience Center (2015–2018); Management Consultant at PwC's Strategy& (2013–2015). He helped start [GrowthDesigners.co](https://growthdesigners.co), a community for growth designers, by creating its Slack community in 2018, and has spent about eight years helping build it to 2,000+ members. He also co-leads [Growth Design School](https://www.growthdesigners.co/school), the community's growth design course.

Education: Brigham Young University (BYU), business strategy, graduated 2013. He moved from management consulting into design and is self-taught as a designer.

Profiles: [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/scottcharleschristensen/) · [X @_ScottC_](https://x.com/_ScottC_) · [GitHub](https://github.com/scottchristensen) · [Medium @ScottC](https://medium.com/@ScottC)

Not to be confused with other people named Scott Christensen, including a painter of the same name. This Scott Christensen is the product and growth designer described on scottchristensen.design.

## At a glance

- **Project:** Mercury Viral Upsell: Layered education lifted new accounts 6%
- **Scott's role:** Lead Growth Designer, Virality (interim)
- **Team:** 3 x Growth Engineers, (no PM — covered PM scope)
- **Year / duration:** 2025 / 2 months
- **Category:** growth

## Overview

Mercury's viral upsell, the page non-Mercury users land on when a Mercury customer sends or requests money, was a slapped-together boilerplate form. I rebuilt the flow with drip education at every touchpoint, a rebranded landing page, and a redesigned success screen. New account conversions from viral entry points rose **+6%** 🎉.

## Background

[Mercury](https://mercury.com) is a fintech serving startups and SMBs. The virality team's job is to turn moments where existing Mercury users intersect with non-Mercury users into acquisition. The biggest of those moments: when a Mercury user sends or requests money from someone outside the platform, the recipient gets an email with a link to claim payment.

I stepped onto the virality team mid-quarter when their designer moved to another team. Three growth engineers, no PM. I picked up where the previous designer had left off and covered PM scope too.

### The problem

The existing viral upsell was bolted on. The email had no real introduction to Mercury, just a generic "enter your name and email to get started" nudge. Clicking through dropped you on an unbranded form, not mobile-responsive, that asked for your bank info up front. The single upsell happened only at the end, after the form was already submitted.

For a non-Mercury user, the whole flow felt like a stranger asking for sensitive info. Conversion to applicant was weak, and we were leaving acquisition on the table from real intent-rich touchpoints: **2.4M payment-receipt emails** to 481k unique recipients, plus 242k payment requests and 103k recipient-onboarding requests over the trailing year.

## Process

### Discovery and framing

The work fell into four distinct surfaces:

1. The notification **email** a non-Mercury user receives
2. The **landing page / form** they hit after clicking through
3. The **success screen** shown after they submit their bank info to get paid
4. The **success transactional email** sent to confirm the submission and re-anchor them on Mercury

The legacy version treated these as one transactional flow. I treated them as a *drip-education campaign*: each surface earns a little more context about who Mercury is and what's in it for the user.

### The initial notification email

Original copy was boilerplate. I added a one-line value-prop intro: *"Mercury is a fintech that ambitious companies use for banking, credit cards, and financial workflows."* Small change, but it sets the floor. By the time someone clicks, they know what they're walking into.

*(Image: Email value-prop refresh (before and after))*

### The landing page

The form was unbranded, not mobile-responsive, and dense. The bigger redesign I wanted, breaking the single form into multiple lightweight steps and rethinking the information architecture, was out of scope for this round. So I made the pragmatic call: ship the rebrand, refresh the content container, and make it mobile-responsive. That last one was a real win because mobile traffic on these viral surfaces is significant and the legacy was desktop-first.

*(Image: Landing page rebrand and mobile-responsive refresh)*

### The success screen

Original was a thin confirmation. I redesigned it with clear hierarchy, restated the brand, and surfaced a few Mercury value props. Finally giving the user a reason to come back as a real Mercury customer instead of treating the interaction as a one-off bank-info dropoff.

*(Image: Success screen redesign with value props)*

I explored a handful of layout and emphasis alternatives through internal feedback and lightweight customer testing before landing on the current implementation.

*(Figma: Success screen alternative explorations)*

### The success transactional email

Once the user submits their bank info, they get a confirmation email. The legacy version was utilitarian, a "you're set" receipt with no follow-through. I rebuilt it with a prominent primary CTA back into the Mercury value prop, plus a secondary action inviting them to explore the product at [demo.mercury.com](https://demo.mercury.com). The email becomes the fourth nudge in the drip, not a dead end.

*(Image: Success transactional email redesign)*

### Killed ideas

The archive had a lot of explorations:

- **Right-rail value props** on the landing page. Killed for v1: too much visual weight before users had basic brand context.
- **Customer logos / ratings / social proof.** Killed for now. Social proof matters once users have a basic mental model of your product; here, users still need *education first*. We tested this hunch and confirmed it.

### Hard call: ship within scope

I wanted to rethink the IA on the banking info form page: break the dense form into a multi-step conversational flow, like the [Focused Funding](../mercury-focused-funding/) work. Couldn't get there in two months with three engineers and no PM. The pragmatic call was to nail the rebrand, mobile responsiveness, and education layering for v1, and queue the IA work for a later round.

## Learnings

### Drip education beats single-shot upsell

The old flow had one upsell at the end. The new flow has small, layered context at every step. The +6% lift came from the cumulative effect, not any one screen. Users coming in cold need a path, not a pitch.

### Right level of polish for the cold-start moment

Social proof, logos, and ratings are powerful when users know what your product is. When they're seeing your brand for the first time, they need clarity, not credentialing. Get the basics in before stacking persuasion patterns.

### Mobile-responsive is table stakes for viral surfaces

If the user is opening the email on their phone (most of them are), every step that follows needs to work on their phone. A desktop-first form is a leak.

### Growth lives in lifecycle, not just product

The lifecycle touchpoints (emails, system notifications, transactional confirmations) are growth surfaces too, not just operational ones. The click-throughs on the email refresh tell me they pulled their weight in the overall lift. Education is hard to attribute cleanly, but the more you prime a user across the journey, the more each touchpoint feels like another beat in the same conversation instead of a one-off transactional moment.

# Mystery Onboarding: case study

- Source URL: https://scottchristensen.design/work/mystery-onboarding/
- Markdown URL: https://scottchristensen.design/work/mystery-onboarding.md
- Site index for agents: https://scottchristensen.design/llms.txt
- Retrieved: 2026-11-09

> Data-driven new user flow. Using a data-driven approach, I redesigned Mystery's native app onboarding and increased adoption by 10%.

## About Scott

Scott Christensen is a growth design leader based in Salt Lake City with 15 years of experience connecting design craft to strategy and growth. He is cofounder of [SendSight](https://sendsight.ai), which automates lifecycle journey insights for growth teams.

Previously: Design Lead, Growth at [Mercury](https://mercury.com) (2023–2025); Head of Product Design at [H1](https://h1.co) (2020–2022); Founding Designer at [Mystery](https://www.trymystery.com) (2019–2020); Lead Designer / Design Manager at Egencia, an Expedia company (2018–2019); Product Designer / Sr. Designer at PwC Experience Center (2015–2018); Management Consultant at PwC's Strategy& (2013–2015). He helped start [GrowthDesigners.co](https://growthdesigners.co), a community for growth designers, by creating its Slack community in 2018, and has spent about eight years helping build it to 2,000+ members. He also co-leads [Growth Design School](https://www.growthdesigners.co/school), the community's growth design course.

Education: Brigham Young University (BYU), business strategy, graduated 2013. He moved from management consulting into design and is self-taught as a designer.

Profiles: [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/scottcharleschristensen/) · [X @_ScottC_](https://x.com/_ScottC_) · [GitHub](https://github.com/scottchristensen) · [Medium @ScottC](https://medium.com/@ScottC)

Not to be confused with other people named Scott Christensen, including a painter of the same name. This Scott Christensen is the product and growth designer described on scottchristensen.design.

## At a glance

- **Project:** Mystery Onboarding: Data-driven new user flow
- **Scott's role:** Lead Product Designer
- **Team:** 1 x PM, 2 x engineers
- **Year / duration:** 2020 / 1 month
- **Category:** growth

## Overview

Using a data-driven approach, I redesigned Mystery's native app onboarding and increased adoption by 10%.

## Background

[Mystery](https://www.trymystery.com/virtual-events) is a Series A-funded entertainment startup that sends users on personalized adventures in their city. The best part? Customers don't know where they're going until they get there.

*(Video: [Mystery promo](https://vimeo.com/391423749))*

#### A Managed Marketplace

Mystery has normal supply-side dynamics, yet the demand-side is managed and hidden to the end user.

###### **Note:** During the pandemic, Mystery pivoted to virtual events.

### So, how does it work?

1. A user signs up and enters preferences
2. Users book a Mystery for a time and date
3. When the time comes, Mystery automatically calls a ride using Lyft Concierge
4. Users get in without knowing where they were going
5. Mystery matches the user to a pre-selected supply (e.g. events, restaurants)
6. Users show up with other Mystery-goers who have similar preferences, for a discounted rate

*(Image: Lyft Concierge ride-flow screenshot)*

### Value Props

Mystery-goers are typically couples who wanted to try something new in their city. **Discovery** was a big value prop. Others included **novelty** and **adventure**, by pushing themselves out of their comfort zone. Lastly, **ease of scheduling** date nights was another value proposition for couples with busy work lives and/or balancing kids.

### The Problem

> We saw a 16% dropoff during the account creation & preferences onboarding flow.

Like most early-stage startups, Mystery's native app onboarding flow had been built hastily at the outset of the company. The new user flow needed to be rethought to...

- Reduce friction to increase signups
- Clearly communicate our value props & updated branding

*(Figma: Onboarding flow (Figma))*

## Process

### Diving into the data

I compared the # of unique native app downloads to the # of unique accounts created. I found that, of the 16% that churned before completing onboarding, 12% fell off before entering their phone number.

> 12% of all new users bailed during the first 5 screens of their onboarding

### UX Audit

Then, I analyzed what was going on in these screens. It was quite apparent that the user was dumped into a flow that felt like a shakedown.

*(Image: Account-creation UX audit screens)*

To further connect-the-dots, we had heard feedback about the tone of the app. One user said, "For promising to be such a fun experience, this app is too straightforward. It has no personality."

### Ideation

While analyzing the flow, I thought to apply a few onboarding principles:

- Use welcome screens to reiterate value props
- Ask only the bare minimum of the user at the outset

*(Image: Suggested account-creation flow)*

The team agreed and decided to initially create a 'shell profile' with just the phone number. If the user were to skip at any other time in the flow, we'd take them to capture their name, birthdate, and email. If they skipped those, at least we had their number and could try to re-engage with SMS reactivation.

Also, we ended up moving the steps where the users can enrich their profile to the very end. That way the user was already invested in adding their preferences -- which was always the most fun part for users.

*(Image: Profile enrichment moved to end-of-flow)*

### Final

We moved super quick. The team made these changes in less than a week. No time for user testing unfortunately -- such is startup life, amirite?

Immediately we saw results. Over the course of the next month, we saw adoption increase by 10%.

*(Figma: Final onboarding prototype (Figma))*

### Outcome

> Signups increased by 10% over the next month and profile completeness went up by 15%. 🎉

## Learnings

### Data informs Design

Data can tell you what is happening and where it's happening. Qualitative analysis can tell you why. The funnel analysis was the perfect way to point me in the right direction.

### Every user onboards

This product work wasn't on our team's radar until we rebranded. It should have been an active convo and measured more often, earlier.

It seems that we tend to forget about the onboarding experience. Yet, it's the ONLY feature that 100% of your users will experience!

### Young brands need great onboarding

When there isn't much brand awareness of your product, onboarding matters even more. The app must reinforce the value it provides, since users won't know.
